title: Advance Care Planning: Values Before Crisis, Decisions When They Become Relevant
bottomLine: Advance care planning is a process of clarifying values, goals and the person who should speak if capacity is lost; it is not a one-time code-status checkbox. Current treatment decisions still require decision-specific capacity, informed consent and the applicable substitute-decision framework.
recognize: Serious illness, frailty, progressive cognitive disease and recurrent hospitalization increase the value of early goals/values conversations.
A capable patient can revise prior wishes and remains the decision-maker for the current decision.
differentiate: Advance care planning differs from present informed consent and from a clinician-written medical order.
A prior wish guides substitute decisions when applicable but does not automatically replace current capable consent.
assessment: Ask what outcomes/abilities matter, unacceptable burdens, understanding of illness trajectory, preferred substitute decision-maker/contact and cultural/spiritual/family considerations.
workup: No laboratory test determines goals; capacity assessment is decision-specific and triggered by uncertainty, not age or diagnosis alone.
management: Document values and decision-maker information in the accessible record, communicate across care settings and revisit after major health changes.
When a current decision arises, obtain consent from the capable patient or legally appropriate substitute according to jurisdiction.
medicationSafety: Medication de-intensification should follow goals/time-to-benefit and current consent rather than a blanket 'comfort care means stop everything' rule.
redFlags: Unclear capacity in a high-stakes decision
Prior expressed wishes not available during crisis
Treatment plan clearly inconsistent with current goals
counselling: Explain that advance care planning prepares for future decisions and supports the patient's voice; it does not force a decision about every future treatment today.
followUp: Revisit after diagnosis/prognosis/function changes and ensure transitions include the most current documentation.
examTrap: Treating an old advance directive as automatic consent/refusal when the patient is currently capable and expressing a different informed choice.
oneLinePearl: Plan values before crisis; obtain consent for the real decision when it arrives.
sourceBasis: Canadian advance-care-planning and substitute-decision practice principles

title: Palliative Care in Geriatrics: Symptoms, Goals, Function, and Family Support Alongside Disease Care
bottomLine: Palliative care is appropriate alongside disease-directed treatment when serious illness creates symptom, decision or caregiver burden. Assess symptoms, function, goals and supports; use proportional symptom treatment and deprescribing while continuing therapies that still provide meaningful benefit.
recognize: Pain, dyspnea, nausea, constipation, fatigue, delirium, anxiety and caregiver distress often coexist and interact.
differentiate: Palliative care is not synonymous with imminent death or stopping all treatment.
New reversible problems such as urinary retention, fracture, infection or medication toxicity still deserve assessment when treatment aligns with goals.
assessment: Assess symptom severity/impact, function, prognosis understanding, goals, caregiver capacity, spiritual/cultural needs and medication burden.
workup: Use tests only when results can change a goal-concordant treatment; avoid burdensome investigations with no plausible benefit.
management: Use non-drug and pharmacologic symptom management, bowel plans with opioids, psychosocial/spiritual support and anticipatory planning.
Refer specialist palliative care for refractory symptoms, complex decisions or high caregiver burden.
medicationSafety: Opioids for serious-illness pain/dyspnea require individualized dose/titration and monitoring; renal function, frailty and prior exposure matter.
Docusate alone is inadequate opioid-constipation prophylaxis; use an effective bowel regimen unless contraindicated.
counselling: Explain that palliative care adds symptom and decision support and can coexist with active treatment.
followUp: Reassess symptoms/goals frequently as illness changes and ensure after-hours/crisis plans are clear.
examTrap: Withholding useful disease-directed therapy solely because palliative care is involved—or ordering burdensome tests that cannot change goal-concordant care.
oneLinePearl: Palliative care adds comfort and clarity; it does not automatically subtract treatment.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Palliative Care recommendations

title: Hypertension in Older Adults: Treat Cardiovascular Risk Without Creating Orthostatic Harm
bottomLine: Older age alone is not a reason to leave hypertension untreated, but frailty, orthostasis, falls, cognitive/functional dependence and treatment burden change how aggressively therapy is titrated. Measure accurately, confirm chronic hypertension and use current Canadian risk-based guidance while monitoring standing symptoms and renal/electrolyte effects.
recognize: Isolated systolic hypertension is common; white-coat effects, autonomic dysfunction and medication-related orthostasis complicate interpretation.
differentiate: Chronic asymptomatic hypertension differs from acute target-organ injury.
A fit independent older adult differs from a frail patient with recurrent falls/orthostatic hypotension despite the same chronological age.
assessment: Use validated standardized BP measurement and home readings when appropriate; assess orthostatic symptoms/BP, falls, frailty, kidney disease, diabetes/CVD, medications and goals.
workup: Use cardiovascular-risk/end-organ evaluation and targeted secondary-cause testing when indicated; monitor creatinine/potassium after relevant therapy changes.
management: Use lifestyle and guideline-directed first-line therapy, often low-dose combinations, while titrating to benefit/tolerability.
Individualize targets/intensity when functional dependence, orthostasis, limited life expectancy or treatment harms dominate.
medicationSafety: Diuretics, alpha blockers and multiple BP-lowering drugs can worsen orthostasis; RAAS blockers/MRAs require renal/potassium monitoring.
Do not abruptly normalize a markedly high chronic BP without target-organ injury.
counselling: Teach home BP technique and to report dizziness/falls rather than stopping all therapy without review.
followUp: Review seated/standing symptoms, home BP and labs after meaningful changes; simplify regimen where possible.
examTrap: Pursuing a low office BP target in a frail patient with recurrent orthostatic falls without reconsidering net benefit.
oneLinePearl: Treat vascular risk, but make standing safely part of the blood-pressure outcome.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada older-adult BP individualization principles

title: Diabetes in Older Adults: Prevent Hypoglycemia, Preserve Function, Individualize Targets
bottomLine: Diabetes treatment in older adults is driven by functional status, frailty, cognition, life expectancy and hypoglycemia risk—not age alone. Fit independent adults may use usual evidence-based targets; frailty/dementia require less intensive targets and active deprescribing of high-risk therapy to avoid hypoglycemia.
recognize: Older adults may have impaired hypoglycemia awareness and present with falls, confusion or weakness rather than classic adrenergic symptoms.
CKD, cognitive impairment, irregular meals and insulin/sulfonylureas markedly increase hypoglycemia risk.
differentiate: High A1C does not guarantee absence of hypoglycemia; CGM/SMBG can reveal wide variability and nocturnal lows.
End-of-life diabetes care prioritizes avoiding symptomatic hyperglycemia and any hypoglycemia rather than A1C normalization.
assessment: Assess function/frailty/cognition, meal reliability, renal function, hypoglycemia history/awareness, glucose data, medication self-management ability, falls and goals.
workup: Use A1C when clinically meaningful and CGM/SMBG according to regimen/risk; reassess kidney function and complications without over-screening when time-to-benefit is limited.
management: Prefer lower-hypoglycemia-risk regimens where possible and simplify treatment for dependence/frailty.
De-intensify insulin/secretagogues when control is too tight or hypoglycemia risk outweighs long-term benefit.
medicationSafety: Sulfonylureas require caution; renal impairment changes many drug/insulin requirements.
Avoid sliding-scale-only insulin as chronic long-term-care management when a safer scheduled/simple regimen is feasible.
counselling: Set goals around safety/function and explain why a higher A1C target may be appropriate without calling it 'giving up'.
followUp: Track hypoglycemia and function more closely than minor A1C changes after de-intensification.
examTrap: Intensifying insulin because A1C is above a younger-adult target despite recurrent nocturnal hypoglycemia and frailty.
oneLinePearl: In frail older adults, avoiding hypoglycemia is a treatment target—not a compromise.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada — Diabetes in Older People

title: Heart Failure in Older Adults: Congestion, Perfusion, Frailty, and Foundational Therapy
bottomLine: Heart-failure care in older adults still uses evidence-based disease-modifying therapy, but congestion/perfusion, kidney function, potassium/BP, frailty, cognition, falls, adherence and goals determine how rapidly and how far treatment can be titrated. Dyspnea/edema should not be assumed to be heart failure without clinical confirmation.
recognize: Orthopnea, PND, edema, elevated JVP, crackles, rapid weight change and exercise decline can indicate congestion; hypotension, cool extremities, oliguria or altered mentation suggest poor perfusion.
differentiate: BNP/NT-proBNP are influenced by age, CKD, obesity and AF and support rather than independently establish HF.
Edema/dyspnea can arise from venous disease, lung disease, anemia, renal disease or deconditioning.
assessment: Assess volume/perfusion, BP/orthostasis, rhythm, renal function, potassium, medication adherence/access, NSAID use, frailty, cognition and goals.
workup: Use ECG, renal/electrolytes, CBC, natriuretic peptides when useful and echocardiography to define structure/EF.
management: Use guideline-directed HFrEF foundational therapies in suitable patients and diuretics for congestion; individualize titration to BP, renal/potassium and frailty tolerance.
Rehabilitation, nutrition, medication simplification and caregiver support are often essential to successful therapy.
medicationSafety: Monitor creatinine/potassium/BP with RAAS/ARNI/MRA changes; SGLT2 therapy requires volume/sick-day context.
Avoid NSAIDs and unnecessary medication burden that worsen congestion/renal risk.
redFlags: Unable to maintain medication/food/fluid plan safely at home
counselling: Teach weight/symptom action plan and medication purpose while aligning treatment complexity with capacity/supports.
followUp: Use close early follow-up after decompensation/titration and reassess function/frailty as well as labs/volume.
examTrap: Withholding all disease-modifying HF therapy because the patient is old—or maximizing doses despite symptomatic hypotension and recurrent falls.
oneLinePearl: Age does not cancel HF benefit; tolerance, frailty and goals determine the safe path to it.

title: Cognitive Screening: Measure Concern, Then Diagnose the Cause and Functional Impact
bottomLine: Cognitive screening is useful when there is a clinical concern or relevant context; it does not diagnose dementia by itself. Interpret the result with education/language/sensory status, collateral history and function, and first exclude delirium or another acute cause when cognition changed suddenly.
recognize: Medication/financial errors, getting lost, repeated questions and functional decline may be more informative than subjective memory complaint alone.
differentiate: Delirium is acute/fluctuating; depression, hearing/vision impairment and medication effects can reduce screening performance.
Normal screening does not rule out subtle executive impairment when function/history is concerning.
assessment: Clarify baseline/trajectory, ADLs/IADLs, collateral history, mood, sleep, medications, sensory impairment, driving/safety and language/education context.
workup: Use a validated cognitive tool appropriate to context and targeted CBC/chemistry/TSH/B12/imaging when the clinical syndrome warrants them.
management: Address reversible contributors and proceed to dementia/MCI evaluation/support when persistent decline is established.
medicationSafety: Reduce anticholinergic/sedative burden before attributing all cognitive symptoms to neurodegeneration.
counselling: Explain that screening is one piece of assessment and does not equal a permanent diagnosis.
followUp: Track function/trajectory and close specialty/support referrals when needed.
examTrap: Diagnosing dementia from one low cognitive score obtained during delirium or without correcting hearing impairment.
oneLinePearl: Screening detects a signal; diagnosis requires trajectory and function.

title: Functional Assessment: ADLs, IADLs, Mobility, and the Tasks That Determine Independence
bottomLine: Functional assessment asks what the person can safely do in real life. ADLs, IADLs, gait/mobility, transfers and cognition/support requirements guide care intensity and discharge more directly than disease count or age.
recognize: IADL decline such as medication, finances, shopping or transportation difficulty can precede basic ADL loss.
Performance can vary with acute illness, environment and available supports.
differentiate: Dependency due to environment/access differs from physical/cognitive inability.
A screening score should not override observed function or caregiver/patient history.
assessment: Assess bathing/dressing/toileting/transfers/feeding plus medications, finances, meals, shopping, housekeeping, phone/technology and transportation; include gait, falls and assistive devices.
workup: Use standardized ADL/IADL/gait/frailty tools when they answer a question; investigate new functional decline for reversible medical causes.
management: Match rehabilitation, home care, equipment, medication simplification and supervision to the specific deficit.
Discharge only when required tasks and supports are realistically available.
medicationSafety: Medication self-management is a functional skill; simplify packaging/schedule or involve supports when cognition/vision/dexterity make the regimen unsafe.
redFlags: Caregiver unable to provide required help
counselling: Frame supports as tools for autonomy rather than proof of failure.
followUp: Reassess after acute illness/rehab and update services as function changes.
examTrap: Discharging a medically stable patient home without checking whether they can transfer, toilet, eat and manage essential medications safely.
oneLinePearl: Medical stability is not functional readiness for discharge.

title: Transitions of Care: Medication Reconciliation, Pending Results, Function, and Ownership
bottomLine: Older adults are vulnerable at transitions because medication changes, functional decline, pending tests and fragmented ownership accumulate. A safe transition reconciles the real medication list, explains what changed and why, confirms function/supports, assigns pending-result follow-up and ensures the receiving team/patient can execute the plan.
recognize: Readmission risk rises with polypharmacy, cognitive impairment, frailty, language/sensory barriers, new equipment and unclear follow-up.
differentiate: A discharge summary is not a completed transition if medication access, pending results or follow-up ownership are unresolved.
assessment: Review pre-admission vs discharge medications, function/cognition, caregiver capacity, transportation, equipment, wound/device needs, nutrition and ability to understand/obtain the plan.
workup: Identify all pending labs/pathology/imaging and explicitly assign who will review/action them.
management: Reconcile medications, stop obsolete duplicates, use teach-back, communicate with primary/specialty/community/LTC teams and arrange timely follow-up.
Use pharmacist/home-care/rehab support for high-risk transitions.
medicationSafety: Explain starts/stops/dose changes and ensure prescriptions are actually accessible; avoid unintentional restart of discontinued inpatient medications.
counselling: Give one understandable medication/action list and concrete return/escalation instructions.
followUp: Use early post-transition contact for high-risk patients and close pending results/referrals.
examTrap: Calling discharge complete because paperwork is signed while three medication lists conflict and no one owns a pending biopsy result.
oneLinePearl: A transition is safe only when the next person knows, can do and owns the plan.

title: Long-Term Care: Frailty, Goals, Infection Stewardship, Function, and Medication Burden
bottomLine: Long-term-care medicine is longitudinal frailty care, not hospital medicine transplanted into a facility. Align treatment with goals and function, prevent delirium/falls/pressure injury, simplify medications, use infection/diagnostic stewardship and avoid burdensome transfers/tests when they cannot improve a meaningful outcome.
recognize: Residents often have dementia/frailty, high medication burden, aspiration risk, mobility/continence issues and atypical illness presentations.
Acute decline can still represent serious disease and should not be dismissed as baseline frailty.
differentiate: Asymptomatic bacteriuria does not warrant antibiotics; nonspecific change without infection evidence needs broader delirium/medical assessment.
Facility care goals may prioritize comfort/function, but reversible symptomatic illness can still merit treatment.
assessment: Track baseline cognition/function, weight/intake, skin, falls, continence, pain, medication burden, goals/substitute decision-maker, caregiver/family context and facility resources.
workup: Order tests only when results can change a goal-concordant plan; avoid routine urine cultures and low-value repeated labs without a clinical question.
management: Use interdisciplinary nursing/pharmacy/rehab/nutrition/palliative approaches, vaccination/infection prevention, pressure/fall prevention and deprescribing.
Transfer to acute care when required treatment/diagnostics or instability exceed facility capability and transfer aligns with goals.
medicationSafety: Avoid sliding-scale-only insulin, chronic sedative-hypnotics and antipsychotic use without narrow indication/reassessment; review medications regularly.
counselling: Discuss realistic facility capabilities, goals and hospitalization preferences before crisis when possible.
followUp: Review function/goals/medication burden after acute events and ensure return-from-hospital changes are reconciled.
examTrap: Sending a urine culture and antibiotics for every episode of confusion in LTC or using sliding-scale insulin alone for convenience despite recurrent hypoglycemia.
oneLinePearl: Long-term care prioritizes function, goals and stewardship while still recognizing true acute illness.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Geriatrics and Long-Term Care principles
